solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

blocks.note: oats boiled in water or milk, a Scottish staple
British slang for a stretch in jail, the time an inmate serves

annotation.surface: A question about what breakfast gets dished up to inmates.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Served' pretends to be about dishing up food; in the second sense it is time served. PORRIDGE is British slang for a spell in prison, and also the title of a classic British prison sitcom.
annotation.definitionFit: Porridge is the oatmeal dish Scotland is famous for.

indicatorNotes.spoiled: something spoiled has had its order ruined, so the letters are scrambled

annotation.surface: A packet that should be pristine has been ruined.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Immaculate' and 'spoiled' look like opposites describing the same sachet; in fact one is the definition and the other the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Immaculate in the moral sense, pure and without stain, is chaste.

blocks.note: fruit whizzed up in a blender

annotation.surface: A smooth operator who mixed a fruit drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Charmer' as the subject of the verb 'blended'; in fact 'blended' belongs to the drink.
annotation.definitionFit: A smoothie is both a smooth-talker and a thick blended drink.

indicatorNotes.short: short means cut off before the end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
DEAL (contract) with its last letter cut off

annotation.surface: A plan for a brief contract.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Short contract' reads as a short-term agreement; 'short' actually tells you to trim DEAL.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a plan you have in mind, as in 'I've an idea for Saturday'.

entries.clue: First of brides I give away is 18 (6)

annotation.definitionNote: 18 refers to the answer to 18 across, CLERIC

indicatorNotes.First of: takes the first letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: to shop someone is British slang for informing on them

annotation.surface: A wedding scene: the father giving away his daughter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Give away' pretends to be the father's role at a wedding; here it means betray. The definition is a cross-reference: 18 across is CLERIC, and a bishop is one.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a bishop is one kind of cleric, a senior one in charge of a diocese.

annotation.surface: The head of the household is at home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chief parent' reads as one phrase; 'Chief' is the definition, an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the adjective: the main road and the chief road are the same one.

indicatorNotes.refurbishment of: a refurbishment rearranges everything, so the letters are reordered

annotation.surface: A shop has had a stylish makeover.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is one idea, a smart shop after a makeover, and the clue's last word supplies its own letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Posh means smart, upmarket, classy.

entries.clue: Admiral excited having penned good song (8)

indicatorNotes.excited: excited letters are stirred up, so they are scrambled
indicatorNotes.having penned: to pen is to enclose, so G goes inside

annotation.surface: An admiral gets worked up after writing a fine song.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Penned' suggests writing the song; it means holding the G inside, as a pen holds sheep.
annotation.definitionFit: A madrigal is a part-song for several voices.

indicatorNotes.in: REST goes in the other piece

blocks.note: PO = Post Office; it holds the break

annotation.surface: A quick break in the post office queue.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quick break' reads as one phrase, a short breather; 'Quick' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Presto is the musical direction for very fast.

indicatorNotes.in: the answer sits in the words that follow

annotation.surface: A capital city in Austria back then was sophisticated: Vienna, you'd think.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface steers you to Vienna, Austria's capital; the capital wanted is the Greek one, strung across three words.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Greece's capital city, one of many capitals the word could point to.

entries.clue: Fringe say combed back on journalist (4)

indicatorNotes.combed back: back tells you to turn EG round
indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, A on B puts A after B

blocks.note: ed = editor, the crossword's standard journalist
e.g. = say, for example; turned round to GE

annotation.surface: A fringe of hair combed back on a reporter's head.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fringe' and 'combed back' paint a hairstyle; 'Fringe' is the definition in its sense of border.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of border or margin, as on the fringe of town.

entries.clue: See hippo splashing about — one spraying water around? (8)

indicatorNotes.splashing about: about means the letters are moved around

annotation.surface: A hippo wallowing in a river, sending water everywhere.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition teases that the hippo itself is 'one spraying water around'; the answer is the garden hose.
annotation.definitionFit: A hosepipe is a thing that sprays water around the garden.

indicatorNotes.working: letters working are busy moving, so they are rearranged

annotation.surface: You need working ears to enjoy a song.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Working' seems to describe healthy ears; it is the instruction to rework the two words before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A serenade is a love song sung beneath a window.

indicatorNotes.New: new means made over, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.fed: a thing fed has something put inside it, so C goes in

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral 100; placed inside

annotation.surface: A new hospital patient is given a hundred peanuts to eat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Peanuts' looks like the food fed to the patient; it is slang for a tiny sum of money.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'paid peanuts' means paid a paltry, trifling amount.

blocks.note: to reap is to cut a crop

annotation.surface: Slice a fruit's skin once more.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fruit's surface' reads as the skin; the ’s is 'is', and 'surface' is a verb meaning come up.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a diver who surfaces again comes back into view.

indicatorNotes.in: ROD goes in the other piece

blocks.note: pay = money earned; it holds the stick

annotation.surface: Put money into a satirical show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stick in' reads as a verb, insert money; 'Stick' is the noun ROD and 'in' the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A parody is a mocking imitation, a form of satire.

indicatorNotes.finally: takes the last letter of love

annotation.surface: Finally, a day filled with love.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Love' tempts you to O, the usual crossword love; 'finally' asks only for its last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to fill someone up with food is to satisfy their appetite completely.

blocks.note: hit, as a snake or an army does
what workers do in an industrial dispute

annotation.surface: Someone lashes out and then storms off.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves read as one angry person's actions; each is a separate sense of the same word, joined by 'and'.
annotation.definitionFit: Strike means both to attack and to stop work in protest.

indicatorNotes.dancing: dancing letters move about, so they are rearranged

annotation.surface: A preacher joins a circle dance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction, but it only links definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: preaching is a priest's job, so a preacher stands for any member of the clergy.

entries.clue: Page left empty, as folio initially (4)

indicatorNotes.initially: takes the first letter of each word

annotation.surface: A page of a book left blank.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Page' is not part of the run: the first letters start at 'left'.
annotation.definitionFit: A leaf is a sheet of a book, its two pages.

entries.clue: Horrific media making me finally shut up (4)

indicatorNotes.finally: takes the last letter of each word

annotation.surface: A plea to lock away awful press coverage that has made someone retreat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' pretends to say 'be quiet'; it means lock in.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to shut up is also to lock in, as a bird is kept behind bars.

entries.clue: Country road originally on back street (6)

indicatorNotes.originally: takes the first letter of road
indicatorNotes.back: going back means travelling the opposite way, so ON is read from its end

annotation.surface: A country lane joining a back street.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back street' reads as one phrase; 'back' belongs to 'on'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Scandinavian kingdom is one country among many.

blocks.note: a pop group is a band

annotation.surface: An ageing pop group all dressed up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dressed' suggests clothes; it means a wound dressed with a bandage.
annotation.definitionFit: A medical sense of the verb: nurses dress a wound by wrapping it.

blocks.note: a buzz, a rush of pleasure

annotation.surface: The excitement of playing football.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma makes it read as a thrill found in football; the two halves are separate senses, the question mark flagging the playful second.
annotation.definitionFit: Getting a kick out of something is getting a thrill from it.
